questions.question_text:
A study was conducted to explore the process and outcomes of a program of occupational activities for patients with dementia. Data from
observations, interviews with patients and sta�, and �eld notes were analyzed to discover the opportunities and barriers to conducting an
occupational program in a day hospital unit. The above study falls under which of the following study designs?
questions.explanation:
The above is an example of qualitative research. Qualitative research largely developed from social research. The important questions that
can be studied qualitatively are; Why people behave the way they do How opinions and attitudes are formed How people are a�ected by the
events that go on around them How and why cultures have developed in the way they have The di�erences between social groups
(Retrieved from  to Research)

questions.question_text: Qualitative methods include all of the following except
questions.explanation:
Census survey refers to a large cross-sectional survey covering the whole, not a sample of a population. These large surveys are more
suitable for quantitative data collection and synthesis; the census is not used as a qualitative research technique.

questions.question_text: In which of the following studies a qualitative approach is most appropriate?

options.text: A comparison of the e�ectiveness of tetrabenazine vs. reserpine in the treatment of tardive dyskinesia.
A survey of number of school teachers exposed to bullying from students and the distribution of mental health problems among those
A multicenter pragmatic naturalistic exploration of all cause discontinuation rates for antidepressants.
An exploration of the role of the 'Community team coordinators' in the elderly community health care teams in the North East of
A national postal survey of doctor's knowledge of prescribing nicotine replacement therapies.

questions.explanation:
Tetrabenazine trial is clearly quantitative. National surveys of knowledge and practice are usually conducted through questionnaires which
collect feeble qualitative information; these are analysed quantitatively on most occasions. The last example is a pragmatic RCT, far from a
qualitative study. Some situations where qualitative research is useful are, 1. When exploring the nature of the problem to be studied; i.e.
before planning quantitative research 2. To generate hypothesis based on observations made. 3. Investigating anomalies or oddities
observed during clinical practice 4. Examining policy implementation 5. Collating service users/ carers/ sta� views.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is generally a feature of qualitative but not quantitative research?
questions.explanation:
Testing a hypothesis, random sampling, controlled interventions or exploration of aetiology and generalising inferences (deductive
approach) are used in quantitative research. Qualitative research uses a purposeful sample, often includes outliers and anomalies, in order
to generate a theory or hypothesis.

questions.question_text: In grounded theory method of qualitative research, the term theoretical saturation is used to describe which of the following?

options.text: Point at which the research hypothesis is fully formed
Point at which the research is stopped
Point at which no new categories can be developed from the available data
Process of checking validity of information using various sources of data
Process of testing new categories using fresh data

correct_answer.text: Point at which no new categories can be developed from the available data

questions.explanation:
The grounded theory refers to a technique of generating theories/categories using qualitative methods. In this technique, i. Initially, a
constant comparison of the collected data takes place in di�erent stages of the data collection. ii. From these comparisons, categories are
generated until nothing new is revealed, i.e. the point of theoretical saturation is reached. iii. Later these categories are tested by collecting
further fresh data on the basis of the new categories made - this is called theoretical sampling.

questions.question_text:
Which of the following methods is the most appropriate to explore the experience and meaning of stigma by schizophrenia patients, their
relatives, and health professionals?

options.text: A case control study with two control groups
A well constructed single self report questionnaire
Participant observation for all three groups individually
Postal survey with rewards for returning the questionnaire

questions.explanation:
Conducting interviews in a group format with some predetermined structure for such groups, in order to provide a focus for discussion, is
called 'focus groups' (Kitzinger, 1995). Focus groups usually contain a small number of members selected giving views on the chosen topic;
the discussion here is semi-structured guided by key points. These are useful in gathering opinions of service users and providers. Postal
surveys and self-report questionnaires do not generate much data needed for adequate understanding of 'life experiences'.

questions.question_text: In which of the following research methods the clear cut demarcation between researcher" and "researched" may not be so apparent?"
questions.explanation:
PAR (or simply action research) involves individuals and groups researching their own personal beings, socio-cultural settings and
experiences. The clear cut demarcation between and 'researcher' and the 'researched' that is found in other types of research may not be so
apparent in action research. For example, a PAR study may involve researchers working with carers of schizophrenia patients to identify
which family or environmental situations provide substantial challenges to the service users. Meyer, J. (2000) Qualitative research in health
care. Using qualitative methods in health related action research. British Medical Journal, 320, 178-181

questions.question_text:
In a research interview, the interviewer does not follow any order but frames the questions on the basis of the interviewee's previous
response. Which of the following style is he following?
questions.explanation:
In structured interviews, a tight schedule of questions may be used with an intention to elicit one of the few limited range of responses,
similar to a questionnaire. Semi-structured interviews (sometimes referred to as focused interviews) involve a series of open-ended
questions based on the topic areas the researcher wants to cover. Though there is a schedule of topics to cover, the exact way questions are
phrased is not premeditated or dictated by a list. Unstructured interviews are also referred to as 'in-depth' interviews where the interviewer
has some limited number of topics in his mind but does not follow any order and frames the questions on the basis of the interviewee's
previous response

questions.question_text:
A researcher organises focus groups to explore the experience of being admitted to an intensive psychiatric care ward. All of the following
will increase the usefulness of the study method except

options.text: More than one focus group is used in the actual project
Having a good degree of group interaction
Having a predetermined topic to discuss at the group
All members of the groups have the common experience of being inpatients in the ward
Each group has around 24 to 36 subjects only

correct_answer.text: Each group has around 24 to 36 subjects only

questions.explanation:
Focus groups are very useful when limited resources prevent individual interviews. They are used when the studied individuals share a
common factor where collecting views of several of them may be useful; these factors should be important to the topic of investigation. If
group interaction may allow greater insights to be developed, focus groups may be used. Members must be usually 6 - 10; it is not a good
idea to have just one group for the whole research - many small groups must be included in the research

questions.question_text: Which of the following terms describe the procedure for producing a written version of a qualitative research interview?
questions.explanation:
Data collection process in qualitative research includes transcribing. Transcribing is the procedure for producing a written version of the
interview. It is a full 'script' of the interview. Transcribing is a time-consuming process. The estimated ratio of time required for transcribing
interviews is about 5:1 (i.e. a 10 minutes interview may need 50 minutes to be transcribed).

questions.question_text: Which of the following clinical questions is better suited to qualitative rather than quantitative research methods?

options.text: A study to measure quality of life in people with Alzheimer's disease.
A study to measure psychiatric symptoms after a head injury
A study of the costs per unit of 'patient utility' in a randomized controlled trial
A study to assess the attitudes of people with borderline personality disorder to their diagnosis
A study detailing the functional outcomes of people treated with Cognitive Behavioural Therapy

correct_answer.text: A study to assess the attitudes of people with borderline personality disorder to their diagnosis

questions.explanation:
The quality of life is often established using standardised questionnaires that test the degree of presumed life quality in samples. Such
questionnaires yield quantitative data for statistical analysis. Patient utility costs are studied using quantitative economic analyses. Study of
attitudes of borderline patients towards their diagnosis is a good example of qualitative design.

questions.question_text: Theoretical sampling is associated with

options.text: Using non-emerging categories for further research
Developing a theory for further research

correct_answer.text: Developing a theory for further research

questions.explanation:
Theoretical sampling is associated with the generation of a new theory for further research. It uses categories that emerge during a
qualitative interview (grounded theory process) to construct the theory. It is not an intuitive method; it does not involve randomisation or
picking up of a convenient sample.

questions.question_text: Qualitative methods are useful in all except:
questions.explanation: Quantitative methods are better suited for evaluating treatment response.

questions.question_text: Qualitative methods include all except:
questions.explanation: A case-control study is a quantitative research method.

questions.question_text: Which of the following can be used to demonstrate the validity of a qualitative study?

options.text: Duration of time spent on research
The signi�cance value derived for primary outcome

questions.explanation:
Re�exivity means sensitivity to the ways in which the researcher and the research process have shaped the collected data, including the role
of prior assumptions and experience, which can in�uence the results. The degree of re�exivity in a qualitative study is used as a method of
assessing the validity of the study. Other methods include triangulation, respondent checking and deviant case analysis. Brown, C and Lloyd,
K (2001). Qualitative methods in psychiatric research. Adv Psych Treatment, 7, 350-356.

questions.question_text: Re�exivity involves:

options.text: Awareness of the patient as a positioned observer in research
Consideration of the impact of the presence of the disease on data collected
Refusing generated theory if any deviant case is noted
Recognition of the researcher's preconceptions and their in�uence on interpretation and analysis

correct_answer.text: Recognition of the researcher's preconceptions and their in�uence on interpretation and analysis

questions.explanation:
Re�exivity means sensitivity to the ways in which the researcher and the research process have shaped the collected data. It includes
recognition of the researcher's preconceptions and their in�uence on interpretation and analysis. Brown, C and Lloyd, K (2001). Qualitative
methods in psychiatric research. Adv Psych Treatment, 7, 350-356.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following techniques is useful in validating data from qualitative studies?
questions.explanation:
Triangulation is a qualitative research technique in which a researcher compares the �ndings of di�erent methods and the perspectives of
di�erent people or groups to help produce a more comprehensive set of �ndings; this is not the same as inter-rater reliability, and does not
necessarily require more than one researcher

questions.question_text: In qualitative studies, semi-structured interviews are often chosen over other forms of interviews. This is because

options.text: Good balance between resource limitations and amount of data collected
Easy accessibility of established interview schedules

correct_answer.text: Good balance between resource limitations and amount of data collected

questions.explanation:
The strengths of the semistructured interview methodology include its ability to balance the need for acquiring good quality data that is
required to investigate complex behaviors and motivations with the limited time available to researchers in the �eld. In addition, semi-
structured interviews have better response rates than a questionnaire survey; are particularly useful when discussing sensitive issues as
they enable the researcher to explore new phenomenon as well as enquire about expected phenomena; achieve good comparability by
ensuring that all items are answered by each participant; ensure that the responses are not in�uenced by group dynamics or assistance
from others; are more informative when there are large variations within the sample groups, regardless of the factors that bring about those
variations. In the presence of such variability, a structured interview might not pick the underlying di�erences while an unstructured
interview may lose focus and fail to answer the primary research question. Leech, B. (2002). Asking questions: Techniques for
semistructured interviews. Political Science and Politics. 35(4):665-668.

questions.question_text: Which of the following research methods is commonly used in qualitative research?
questions.explanation: Ethnography involves immersing oneself in a particular social group.

questions.question_text:
You are preparing a study involving a focus group of mental health occupation therapists, exploring their views of memory clinic
assessments. Which of the following is the most important factor to consider for reliability?

options.text: Ensuring the occupational therapists are a representative sample
Ensuring all the occupational therapists have the same amount of experience with memory clinics
Using more than one researcher to facilitate the focus group
Facilitating the group so that there is not too much discussion amongst participants
Using more than one researcher to code the data

correct_answer.text: Using more than one researcher to code the data

questions.explanation: Reliability in a qualitative study can be improved by triangulation and member checking.

questions.question_text: Theoretical sampling is associated with

options.text: Using non-emerging categories for further research
Developing a theory for further research

correct_answer.text: Developing a theory for further research

questions.explanation:
Theoretical sampling is often considered to be the hallmark of grounded theory methodology. It involves the use of emerging categories
using an iterative process to re�ne the theory developed from the data.

questions.question_text:
Woolf et al., BMJ 2008; 337. 27 year 3 medical students and 25 clinical teachers at a London medical school, selected for required ethnicity
and sex, participated in a study that used semistructured one to one interviews and focus groups. Ethnic stereotypes of UK medical
students were explored in the context of academic underachievement of medical students from ethnic minorities. Overall, 26 of 40 clinical
teachers agreed to be interviewed (65%), 12 did not answer, and two declined: one was too busy and one did not give a reason. Of the 49
students invited to participate, 21 agreed to be interviewed (43%). Twelve interviews took place—six with white students and six with
students from ethnic minorities. Five of the students were men and seven were women. High achievers were more likely to attend the focus
groups than low achievers (19.3% v 9.0% of those invited). The Pakistani/Bangladeshi lower achieving group had to be abandoned as a result
of non-attendance. Data were analysed using the theory of stereotype threat (a psychological phenomenon thought to negatively a�ect the
performance of people from ethnic minorities in educational contexts) and the constant comparative method. Throughout the analysis the
interpretation was compared with the verbatim data. Opposite examples were sought and used to re�ne the analysis. Participants believed
the student-teacher relationship was vital for clinical learning. Teachers had strong perceptions about "good" clinical students (interactive,
keen, respectful), and some described being aggressive towards students whom they perceived as quiet, unmotivated, and unwilling.
Students had equally strong perceptions about "good" clinical teachers (encouraging, interested, interactive, non-aggressive). Students and
teachers had concordant and well developed perceptions of the "typical" Asian clinical medical student who was considered over-reliant on
books, poor at communicating with patients, too quiet during clinical teaching sessions, and unmotivated owing to being pushed into
studying medicine by ambitious parents. Stereotypes of the "typical" white student were less well developed: autonomous, con�dent, and
outgoing team player. Direct discrimination was not reported. This investigation suggested that the Asian clinical medical students may be
more likely than white students to be perceived stereotypically and negatively, which may reduce their learning by jeopardising their
relationships with teachers. The existence of a negative stereotype about their group also raises the possibility that underperformance of
medical students from ethnic minorities may be partly due to stereotype threat. The sex, ethnicity, and age of the interviewer (British
female, white) may have a�ected participants' discussion of certain topics. The investigator perceived that white clinical teachers who had
positive views about white female medical students and rather more negative views about Asian or male medical students felt comfortable
discussing these views with her in a way that they may not have had she been an Asian medical student. What type of study has been
conducted?
questions.explanation: This is a qualitative study. Note the terms – 'semistructured', 'focus groups' and 'constant comparative' method.

questions.question_text:
Which of the following research techniques used during a qualitative study can inform the number of participants necessary for a given
sample?
questions.explanation:
Saturation is a research technique that is used during a qualitative study to inform the number of participants necessary for a given sample;
data are analysed concurrently with data collection, and the sample is said to be saturated (so data collection can cease) when new themes
stop emerging from the data that have already been gathered. Resonance is a term employed to describe the extent that �ndings from
